questions.q: What are the three official discussion questions listed at the end of the chapter (page 65-66) under "ikB osQ vkl&ikl"?
questions.a: The three questions are: (1) Compare Eksgu's life in the village (xk¡o) and the city ('kgj) – what is the difference? (2) Analyze Thakur Phul Singh's character as a feudal lord – discuss his traits and flaws. (3) The story begins with a flashback (analepsis) – could there be another narrative starting point? questions.q: Explain in your own words why the discussion point "Eksgu does not consider Thakur his master (izfr}a}h)" is central to the story's theme of resistance.
questions.a: Eksgu's refusal to accept Thakur as "malik" (master) despite physical violence and economic dependence signifies an internal psychological liberation that precedes external freedom. It transforms him from a passive victim of "tkfrxr ghurk" (caste pride) into an active agent denying the ideological foundation of feudalism. A wrong answer focusing only on "he was beaten but didn't obey" misses the conceptual leap: the discussion point is about the *ideological* rejection of the master-slave dialectic, not just behavioral disobedience.

questions.q: Apply the discussion framework "Point-Evidence-Explanation-Link (PEEL)" to the prompt: "Discuss the role of the city ('kgj) as a space of anonymity vs. the village (xk¡o) as a space of caste surveillance." Use one evidence from page 60-61.
questions.a: **Point:** The city offers Eksgu anonymity that the village denies. **Evidence:** On page 60-61, when Eksgu returns after education, the narrator notes: "lkekU; rkSj ls czkã.k Vksys osQ yksxksa dk f'kYidkj Vksys esa mBuk&cSBuk ugha gksrk Fkk" (It wasn't common for lower-caste people to move freely in upper-caste areas). **Explanation:** In the village, spatial movement is policed by caste; in the city, the same physical act (walking on a road) becomes unremarkable. **Link:** This contrast structures the story's argument that caste is a spatial-political construct, not an inherent trait. A wrong answer quoting only the village scene without the comparative city reference fails the "Apply" requirement of using the framework on a new comparative prompt.

questions.q: Analyze how the discussion point on Thakur Phul Singh's "fo|kO;luh" (hypocrisy/pretentiousness) connects to the broader theme of "feudal modernity" in the story. Reference his treatment of Eksgu's education vs. his own sons' education.
questions.a: Thakur embodies "feudal modernity" by adopting modern symbols (English education for sons, court cases) while retaining feudal mindsets (caste violence, denying Eksgu's humanity). Evidence: He sends sons to English school (page 58: "f=kyksd flag ekLVj us mls iwjs LowQy dk ekWuhVj cuk j[kk Fkk") but uses Eksgu's education as a tool for better servitude ("eksgu yyk cpiu ls gh cM+s cqf¼eku Fks" – page 62). The discussion point reveals that for Thakur, modernity is instrumental (consolidating power), not transformative (dismantling hierarchy). A wrong answer listing Thakur's "good deeds" (giving food) without analyzing the power dynamic behind them shows inability to separate textual detail from thematic pattern.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The most effective discussion point for a Class 11 board exam oral assessment is Question 2 (Thakur's character) because it allows maximum textual evidence." Defend or challenge with criteria for "effectiveness" in CBSE Speaking assessment.
questions.a: **Challenge.** Effectiveness in CBSE Speaking (ASL) is judged on: (1) Range of vocabulary (Question 1 on village vs city allows richer spatial/emotional lexicon), (2) Structural coherence (Question 3 on narrative structure tests meta-cognitive skill), (3) Critical thinking (Question 2 risks becoming a character sketch without thematic depth). Question 2 is *easiest* to evidence but not most *effective* for demonstrating higher-order skills. A student agreeing without criteria reveals exam-oriented instrumentalism rather than understanding assessment objectives.

questions.a: **Prompt:** "On page 63, Eksgu carries his mother's g¡lqos to the city and later uses it to pin down the snake threatening Thakur's son. How does this object transform from a symbol of caste-assigned labor to an instrument of agency across generations? Discuss with reference to Eksgu's mother, Eksgu, and the Thakur's lineage."
